title: Friends of one another
hook: believing men and women are protectors of one another (9:71)

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhat an-nitaqayn, and the quiet helpers around the cave. Your line was small, brave, ordinary things in the dark.
screen: `SMALL, BRAVE, ORDINARY THINGS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Start with grammar. An Arabic plural like "the believers" can cover a mixed group, the way "you all" does. But in some places the Qur'an says it twice: men and women, believing men and believing women. At-Tawbah does it in verse seventy-one, right after a passage about the hypocrites, men and women, who egg each other on toward wrong. Then the surah turns and describes the other kind of community, and gives it a word: awliya'. Friends. Allies. People who stand at each other's side.

Pickthall translates the verse's opening this way: "And the believers, men and women, are protecting friends one of another; they enjoin the right and forbid the wrong". It goes on: they keep up the prayer, they pay the zakat, they obey God and His messenger, and God will have mercy on them. Awliya' is the plural of wali. Its root, w-l-y, carries the sense of being near, close enough to turn toward. So a wali is a friend, but also an ally, a guardian, someone who has your back. The same word can describe God's closeness to believers, and in another verse, a guardian in a family. Here it runs sideways, between people. And look at the list. Men and women share every verb: both encourage good, both push back on wrong, both pray, both give. The verse doesn't divide the work and hand half to each. Why name both at all? A report in Ahmad's Musnad gives one answer. Umm Salama, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, asked him: why are men mentioned in the Qur'an, and we are not? Later, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, in Surah al-Ahzab. It names ten qualities, each one twice: Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women, truthful men and women, patient, giving, fasting, men and women who remember God much. For all of them, forgiveness and a great reward. A woman asked a question, and the answer came back spelled out ten times over. Scholars disagree about many details of how men and women work together. This verse is a common starting point: protectors of each other.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN, PROTECTING FRIENDS.` · `W-L-Y — NEAR, AT YOUR SIDE.` · `THE SAME VERBS FOR BOTH.` · `UMM SALAMA ASKS; TEN PAIRS COME.` · then, large: `PROTECTORS OF EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone of the other sex in your life: a sister, a brother, a colleague, a classmate, a neighbor. Is there a place where their good idea went unheard, or their work was credited to someone else? Picture standing at their side, speaking up for the right thing, simply and decently; if you pray, ask for that person by name.
Awliya'. Friends, allies, protectors, from a root that means to be near. Believing men and women, at each other's side. Today's word.
Your line: protectors of each other. The same verbs for both. Day four hundred twenty-three, counted.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 9:71 when speaking of shared responsibility between men and women in faith and community life; how that cooperation is arranged in mosques, schools and families varies between scholars and communities.

chat.says: Does the Qur'an only talk to men about doing good in the community?
options: No. 9:71 calls believing men and women protecting friends of one another.
Yes. Women are included silently; the Qur'an never names them directly.
No. But it gives men the good deeds and women only the prayers.
